PhD/Applications/Bodies-in-Digital-Trans.title: Bodies in Digital Transition
PhD/Applications/Bodies-in-Digital-Trans.content:
In the style of… Appropriation, AI, and Unstable Authorship
This research examines how fine artists use cinematic genre tropes and visual motifs in moving image work and photography, how authorship is conceptualised when working with techniques including appropriation and pastiche, and how working with AI-generated content complicates these issues further.
While the deliberate appropriation of existing images, styles, or motifs from other works and cultural sources is a well documented creative method, this approach appears to be an increasing aspect of works which use prompt based and generative ai systems as a tool. Rather than a deliberate critique or contextualisation of the original materials, AI image tools often recreate the visual style of individuals and movements, potentially without the intention, or the understanding of the artist making a new work.  In the context of a technologically engaged visual practice, I’m interested in how artists approach copying, pastiche, homage, remix, appropriation, ripping, quotation and recontextualisation, and where the differences between these practices lie.
This research spans appropriation theory, cinematic genre studies, AI aesthetics, theories of voice and style, and questions of dissemination and communal reception. It is grounded in a personal arts practice characterised by what might be called a magpie relationship with style, constitutively inconsistent, moving between registers without claiming (or necessarily desiring) mastery of any. This paper describes the early stages of a practice based PhD in Arts and Computational Technology at Goldsmiths UoL.
Please submit a short biography 50-150 words
Katie Tindle is a multidisciplinary artist, researcher and founder member of the collective, In-grid. Her recent research focuses on how re/use of tropes and genre conventions function in the context of a critically technologically engaged arts practice. She is a lecturer in Computational Arts at Goldsmiths, University of London, where she is also currently a Doctoral Candidate and member of the Process Iteration Network. More info: katietindle.co.uk/ in-grid.io/

PhD/Applications/Transmediale-2027.title: Transmediale 2027
PhD/Applications/Transmediale-2027.content:
Notes:
Interstices: Research (in) the gaps
Gaps between social cultural and computational structures
What moves through them and do they carry transformative power?
The Dark Forest Theory of the Internet investigates how intelligence–human and artificial–manifests under conditions of secrecy, hostility, and concealment.
Different spaces of habitation
for Konior, the dark forest is increasingly inhabited by other-than-human intelligences that opt for non-engagement with people.
Intended contribution/abstract and relevance to workshop (200 words)
This paper begins with a haunting. When GenAI systems produce moving/image work, style and narrative convention recur without traceable citation. Appropriation, pastiche, and détournement are established practices with critically articulated relationships to their sources. Fan cultures also copy knowingly, openly, and communally, building shared vocabularies of reference [1]. GenAI systems, by contrast, reproduce convention as a byproduct of obscurely curated data models, an interstitial site the structure produces but does not claim. Original contexts are hidden behind this broader opacity that Konior [2] locates in AI systems more widely, where concealment rather than disclosure becomes a mark of intelligence itself.
Rather than treating this only as a loss of authorial control, I want to ask what it opens up. Can this ownerless recurrence be redirected into appropriation in its fullest sense, as deliberate remix or détournement? Can GenAI become a tool for productive misreading rather than passive extraction?
I propose reading this condition through the gothic: a genre historically preoccupied with unstable authorship, from Walpole’s [3] fraudulent framing of The Castle of Otranto as a found manuscript onward, and with architectures of hidden, unindexed space, doubles, dopplegangers and secret histories.

[1] Abby Kirby, “Examining Collaborative Fanfiction: New Practices in Hyperdiegesis and Poaching,” Humanities 11 (2022): 87.
[2] Bogna Konior, The Dark Forest Theory of the Internet (Cambridge: Polity, 2025).
[3] Guy Debord and Gil Wolman, “A User’s Guide to Détournement” (1956).
[4] Horace Walpole, The Castle of Otranto (1764).
Details of current research project (100 words)
I am in the early stages of a practice-based PhD in Arts and Computational Technology at Goldsmiths, University of London. The research traces how fine artists working in moving image and photography inherit, appropriate, and pastiche cinematic genre  and how GenAI complicates that inheritance, returning style and trope without an author to claim them. The research is grounded in a magpie-ish personal arts practice which moves between registers without settling into a single voice. The project reads this condition through the gothic: haunting, forgery, and unstable authorship as tools for thinking through what it means to work with a system that copies without knowing it copies.
Biography
Katie Tindle is a multidisciplinary artist, researcher and founder member of In-grid: a London-based trans * feminist collective of artists/educators/technologists working in and around digital infrastructure. She is a lecturer in Computational Arts at Goldsmiths, University of London, and where she is also currently a Doctoral Candidate and member of the Process Iteration Network. She also teaches at University of Arts London, BA Fine Art: Computational Art.

PhD/Misc-notes-and-diaries/Description-f.content:
Written April 1st 2026
I am interested in how fine artists use genre tropes and visual motifs in moving image work, and in photography, and what the implications of working with AI to generate moving image work are. While artists have often worked with cinematic language in moving image work and photography, this appears to be an increasing aspect of works which use prompt based ai as a tool (for making images, voice overs, scripts) without acknowledging the that they are mimicking existing works, with exceptions (Duck by Rachel McClean for instance, Adam Cole). I’m exploring how use of cinema, literary and pop culture tropes function in the context of a technologically engaged practice. While generative text, footage and voice performances enable artists to convincingly mimic, there is has been less discussion of what these factors activate in combination with each other.
I’m interested in how artists approach copying, pastiche, homage, remix, appropriation, ripping etc. What are the borders between copying, remixing, reappropriation or ghost writing. What the practices of sampling, remixing, meming and theft, pastiche, fan fictioning do and what the differences are. There is also legal/copywrite implication that I am interested in exploring at a later point I think.
I’m also working to articulate my own practice which has a Magpieish relationship with style. For example I have made works which use tropes of gothic horror, copypasta, medical language, folk story.
Related to this, I’m also interesting in looking at how are artist’s essays and films disseminated, and via what platforms and methods. Why does it matter that these things are communal – this is an open question to me, but something about the intentionality of fan fiction to mimic a particular property or trope is interesting to me.

PhD/Misc-notes-and-diaries/Genre-hopping.title: Genre hopping
PhD/Misc-notes-and-diaries/Genre-hopping.content:
Already in the process of starting this project I’ve been hopping about from topic to topic. Always circling the same area - writing as a method and an outcome, films, genres. At first I thought I cared about the idea of emulating artist essays. That being said, I think its the emulation in general I care about rather than the essay itself. An adoption of style to garner a particular type of status, or reading. It can be, or has been something that I have been self conscious of - my magpie approach to topics and methods. A jack of all trades. But rather than worry about it too much now, and worry that I’ll lose interest and wander off, I’m going to try and stay with that idea of moving and attempt to see what’s interesting about it.
I’m interested in understanding what the appeal is of using certain tropes, or memes, or rhetorical devices to emulate another person’s style, or the style of a genre. It’s something I occasionally do as part of my practice, where I have an idea I want to express, and so choose the voice I want to use to express that. I am tool and medium agnostic in that way, and this can make my practice hard to define. This has felt uncomfortable at times, when it can be useful and marketable to be easily defined and understood. Short, snappy and easily digested.
Why use another’s voice? Is it less authentic than developing something distinct? Is there anything distinct anyway? (see hauntology). For me there is an invitation in choosing a genre to emulate which invites the audience to read what I am giving them in a certain way. I’ve told you this is horror, read it as horror. In that way it feels more authentic, more in keeping. Is there something interesting in being un-markatably inconsistent, or emulating so closely you start to infringe on copywrite?
I would like to develop a methodology for this hopping from topic to topic, from style to style. What can be generative about inconsistency? Am I interested in the shifting between genres, or the genres themselves?
Why do we want to copy style, and what is there in a refusal to be the author in that way, a ghost writer.
Could it be a form of drag? I have no house style - would it be possible for someone to copy me. It would be interesting to find out from people who know me and my work decently well (who? In-grid?) to try and understand what I make?
What are the cadences of this moving through different genres or methods. Is it that a question has been answered? Am I just bored? What are the entrances and exits from a particular genre, or a particular question I want answered.
Sampling, remixing, infringing on copyright.
I’m repeating myself.

Genre: Is a catagorisation, or grouping of things, often media and art by shared style, form or content. It’s used to define a thing by what its like, rather than other factors like when it was made or by whom. It is a category that allows a viewer/listener/reader to know what to expect from that piece of media. Some genre’s are hyper specific, or can contain sub-genres (Heavy Metal: Thrash, Death, Black, Nu etc). Some are reductive (world cinema). A tool for classifcation.
Trope: A recognisable pattern or idea that shows up again and again in a particular media, often associated with film and literature. They might belong, or be more prevalent in a particular genre. They might be a plot element, phrasing, character type, situation, visual or stylistic habit. They can be used as short hand, and can be subverted. They can be comforting, or cliche depending on how they are used.
Motif can be specif to one work, and can differ in form across the work - more like a theme.
Style: Is the distinctive way something is expressed or presented. It is used to describe how something is done, not what it is or what it contains. It might refer to language and tone, visual choices, technique and material choices. It might refer to these things in combination.
What are the dependancies (capitalist dependancies) that these genre’s are forced into (top down).
Genre crossing and bending, queering of genre. Horror and B movie sub/counter culture.

PhD/Practice/Creative-writing/Gun-pop.title: Gun pop
PhD/Practice/Creative-writing/Gun-pop.content:
I felt sweaty and smelled sugary - of partially digested spirits and gun pop. A second sugar spike, a watery morning sun and dehydration conspired to wake them up – like a mother, for their own good “drink something”, chastising “what did you drink?”.
I woke up and saw everything too clearly. I had slept wearing
contact lenses limpit-clinging onto my eye balls, which felt
sucked on and bruised. With a low throb of guilt I raked around the floor next to the bed looking for saline solution, knocking over a glass of ordinary, bacteria riddled tap water in the process. Balanced on one elbow I blinked it in – ‘this should loosen them up and they’ll slide right off. Hopefully’. Blasé, I try not to think about corneal ulcers.
Once, new to contact lenses, I had rubbed my eye in the cinema. It had been an early date I think, with a boyfriend who I envision foggily to my left although I couldn’t tell you if it were David or Kieran. We were watching a film. Suddenly my right eye looked at the screen as if through a Vaselined camera lens. It felt like the popcorn in my stomach had
suddenly sucked up all the Pepsi and bile sitting in there with it. I was convinced that I had pushed the lens behind my eyeball. I rose, panicked, to the ladies - my good eye leading the way.
Good eye still reeling from the transition from the dark screening room into an aggressively well-lit bathroom, I stooped over a sink, face inches from the mirror. Eyelid pulled up, I looked for an edge of plastic to tease from behind my eye. I rubbed my salted popcorn fingers on the whites of my eyes until they were laced with red. Finally, hands on the faux marble sink top I calmed
myself – I must have rubbed the lens right out of my eye in the first place and it will be lying ruined on the sticky cinema floor. It’s not in there and now my eye hurts from prodding. I returned to the cinema screen and watched the film half blind. Some twenty minutes later I blinked and the lens descended from above, deus ex machina. As when the optician puts a new disk in the test glasses my vision was restored.
I’d freaked out about a contact lens going behind my eye before I had it happen. Same as I freaked out about them adhering them to my eyes if I accidentally slept in them. Same as I was terrified of getting toxic shock system if I slept with a tampon inserted. Now I do them all, all the time.
I get the disks of thin plastic off their eyes eventually, and withrelief settled into a familiar blur. The plastic was harder now on their fingertip than when they went in. I absentmindedly put the lens on the tip of my tongue. Saline
solution correctly tastes of salt water. Their eyes still felt like
they have sand trapped behind the lids. Cold eyedrop tears run mutely down their face, then neck and are absorbed in the collar of their already grubby sleeping tshirt, soft with sweat.
A short battle raged between lying down and staying still, and needing a piss and needing water. The liquids won out.
Uncomfortably cold around the neck from the cooling sweat and saline solution, they took a ginger walk with bare feet towards the toilet. Collecting mystery bruises from doorways on the way, they relieved themselves and stood with their eyes closed in the cold bathroom, feeling the air between them and the wall and the floor.
I felt crispy and hollow, nausea slowly lapping at the shore and threatening to crest. My headache the more immediate issue. I had stood too quickly from the toilet and the momentum had smashed my brain against the inside of my skull. I remembered a friend who had once held a brain for work that the inside of your skull is actually full of little spikes and that the fluid in there is partly to stop your brain from being raked along them. I image when I’m dehydrated the fluid surrounding my brain depletes and my brain is stretched out like it’s a vacuum and its filling in the space.
Chugging stale water from a pint glass stolen by some previous tenant and they imagined it trickling into their dehydrated brain, filling up their tissues like a magic “grow your own boyfriend” sponge in water. After they felt human enough to look for their glasses. Finding them lens down (shit) on the coffee table, they put them on. The flat came into focus – ish, behind a film of slimey finger prints. They gave them a cursory rub with the edge of their tshirt and replaced them.
Padding back to their bedroom their foot skidded out from
under them on a patch of something slimey on the lino floor and nearly had them set their neck. They examined the patch. It was colourless but iridescent, thicker than water. Glancing round to establish the cause they noticed a pattern of wet patches coming from their bedroom. Quizzical they made to stand, using the wall to steady themselves. Their hand left an oily, iridescent smear.
Repulsed they sprung away and held their palms out in front of them, making their hungover head throb. Turning to make their way to the bathroom their eye was caught by what they had earlier missed. Slimey hand and foot prints covered the flat. Oily and magpie shiney the liquid had seeped into the upholstery of the chairs, was smeared on the doorframe.
What the fuck did you do? There’s no one home, all you did was watch some shit after you got in, still a bit tipsy from the pub and fall asleep on the sofa. They remembered waking up in the night and blearily taking off their work stuff and pulling on an old tshirt from some uni thing. Looking down at their shirt its kind of shining too, even. Their skin is too. Panicked they suddenly feel hot and breathless.
Wheeling to the bathroom, whatever is it, they’re sweating it out.
‘You could be pregnant, make an appointment with your GP’.
That’s impossible.
‘Bacterial infection’ ‘Flu’ ‘Cancer’
Water coming from the taps is marbled.
What did I drink?

PhD/Practice/Creative-writing/Jaw-readin.title: Jaw reading
PhD/Practice/Creative-writing/Jaw-readin.content:
Dull warm even in rest I am here today to talk to you about
strained bits and grind.
Ground like cornmeal and glue, grind like fish bones only a little bit. A deer jaw washes up on a beach white clean from the sandblasting and salt crisp sea.
The lamb sheep deer jaw is sitting in a spot not immediately
visible from cracked black pepper and sea salt crystal sand. The rest of the bones loosely held together by tendons, wool and plastic are also not visible from where we are standing but I wouldn’t bother looking for it as the jaw is a more interesting (read: easier) still life subject.
I put plastic in my mouth so that my fissure ceilings don’t fall out and I don’t give myself a tension headache. I am also afraid the sea might carry my sandcastle teeth in the drift and take them to bleach a baby lamb jaw. Or else take them to crash up against the sea wall to grate against the pitted stone.
Just think what you could keep in there and who might grow in there.
If I were to hook behind my back teeth and instead of popping pull forward, the teeth in there would be wiped away like excess sand from a bucket, the roots packed densely in the jaw. If you were to use a mouth rock tumbler would the rocks or your teeth look prettier, smoothed, the roots of the sandcastle teeth skimmed neatly at the top?

PhD/Practice/Creative-writing/Skeleton-s.title: Skeleton story
PhD/Practice/Creative-writing/Skeleton-s.content:
Text from a performance with Irini Kalaitzidi irinikalaitzidi.com/projects/skeleton-story.html
OCT 25
Would you like to hear my skeleton story? 
Kari sits at her dressing table and skirts her hands delicately over the items arranged in front of her. Waxy face paints in palettes and sticks, cheap, brittle sponges and face wipes. She hadn’t been living in the area long, having moved abruptly after everything that had happened in the Summer. No, she wasn’t going to think about that, that was a different Kari. So, when she had been asked to attend a Halloween party by a new workmate, Charlotte, she was determined to make a good impression. She’d looked at Charlotte’s social profiles just to get an impression of what kind of event it would be. She scrolled carefully through the feed and considered what she found. Charlotte painted in neon patterns at a festival, Charlotte in full black swan costume at what looked like a house party, Charlotte dressed as sad clown the year before. She looked happy, popular, wide eyed and bright. Charlotte took events like this seriously, so Kari would take it seriously too.  
She took a palette of white cream paint in her hand, swirling the rough sponge on its surface before starting the process of turning her face bone white. She wanted this to be perfect, a flawless skull, shadows carved deep around the eyes. She worked slowly, applying layer over layer. Moving to the black paint, her reflection seemed to hollow as she worked, cheekbones sharpening, eyes and lips widening into a rictus grin. The paint was uncomfortable, cold, tacky, almost wet. It smelled of plastic and oil, with an undercurrent sharply smelling of iron. The cheap solution began to sting, the mirror fogged with her breath. The course sponge caught on the fragile skin of her face, feeling it catch, she winced but she worked through the discomfort. Her face pulled under the drag of the sponge and over time stiffened until she could hardly change her expression.  
She inspected her face through the haze of the mirror. Her grin wider than it had been in a long time. She went to the bathroom and washed her hands of the paint, carefully pulling matter from underneath her fingernails. She threw on the rest of her costume, and headed to the party. The chilly autumn air stung a bit deeper as she made her way to Charlotte’s home, but she reasoned this was because the paint was still a little wet, dampening the collar of her shirt.  
Inside, the music pounded, the house filled with people drinking, laughing, leaning into each others spaces, hot breath on ears as people struggled to be heard. A devil threw his head back laughing, and turned to catch Kari’s eye. His laughter died in his throat, eyes widening in barely contained panic. His hand gripped on the shoulder of the vampire he’d been speaking with, who in turn followed the path of his staring eyes to Kari. His skin, turned visibly paler under a patchy layer of talcum powder and his jaw hung loose.  
She grinned. It stretched too far. She swung away, she had done so well. 
She serenely joined the queue to bob for apples. When it was her turn to bob, she plunged her head into the cold water. She felt the water rush into sinuses unpleasantly, her skin felt numb, slippery. She caught an apple between her mouth, and emerged grinning and victorious, the apple caught in sharp teeth. She felt eyes on her and triumphantly bit down. When she swallowed, the chunk slid through her throat and fell out somewhere near her collarbone with a soft, wet tap on the floor. 
Someone screamed. Kari just looked down. The water rippled with her reflection - not painted anymore, but bare, gleaming. The edges of torn skin framing her skull, eyes rolling wide in their sockets. 
She’d done it perfectly. The best skeleton costume she’d ever made. 
Thank you, we needed an audience to verify we have a skeleton

PhD/Practice/Creative-writing/They-were-.title: They were expected to see what stuff she was made of
PhD/Practice/Creative-writing/They-were-.content:
An older work from 2021/2
She drank and felt the rod of cold liquid slide down her gullet like she were swallowing a sword. She was to be made transparent – or translucent. Mostly see-through.
In the seeing through and from certain angles, aspects of her
wholeness or holeness could be assessed.
They were expected to see what stuff she was made of, what
jelly covered what oysters of muscle and sinew. Where the gaps were and which of them were filled and with what. The grit of bones are almost white, the flesh a little darker and the holes a black shadow in what should be solid.
The gaps are important and they made her partially see through-able so these holes could be measured. They wished they could plunge their hands into the gap and feel out those pockets. Like a faith healer they would slide around filling and stretching.
A haste feeler. Two thumbs into the centre and wrench apart.
However, finger tips, like a tongue, make textures feel so much larger than reality. This way the measurements would be much more precise.
She was translucent and her holes and gaps were black. Blue like on the screen she was inside herself looking at the insides of herself in blue.
In the time before the procedure she was to keep completely
still. If she moved her eyes quickly, as when reading, her eyeballs would light up brighter than bone and give them an excuse to pluck them out. She tried not to thinking too quickly.
Her holes and gaps would be compared to others. Little was
known about what formed them, what eroded the insides. Some suggested it was environmental, some a punishment from God. Some even suggested it was the test itself which caused the holes to appear but there had been gaps before the test. People had crumbled like bath bombs in water on the street, like cinder toffee dropped by a child.
What could they see in there? What did those black points say? Were they vacuums or filled with bad air, to be let out using a knife and the tube of a biro like in the movies? Scientists were undecided. Some thought they could be filled but others thought that this would cause more collapse. One man claimed to have filled all his holes, and orifices with a paste made from a paste made of ground linseed, turmeric and a nontoxic latex. Few speculated that some holes were supposed to be there – by design – but most people thought they were quacks. She wondered as she watched herself pink, ‘Do I breathe out these particles of my own self, like calories on my breath. Do the particles of radiation fired at me from across the room punch holes through.
Is it bad?
Slice me open if you want to see if I’m whole or holed, I guess.”

Here are six gothic story premises:
1. The Inherited House
A woman inherits a decaying estate from an aunt she never knew, only to discover the will requires her to live there for a full year before she can sell it. The portraits in the hallway seem to rearrange themselves each night, and the locals refuse to say why the previous owner never left the grounds alive.
2. The Physician’s Ward
A doctor at a remote Victorian asylum becomes obsessed with a patient who claims to remember her own death. As he digs into the asylum’s records, he finds his own name in ledgers dating back a hundred years, in handwriting identical to his own.
3. The Drowned Bride
On the eve of her wedding, a bride finds an old wedding dress in the attic, still damp, that fits her perfectly. As the wedding approaches, she begins losing time, waking near the lake with no memory, while guests whisper about the groom’s first fiancée, who vanished the same way.
4. The Cartographer’s Debt
A mapmaker is hired to survey a fog-bound coastal village that appears in no official records and disappears from any map drawn of it within a week. He accepts a night’s lodging from a gracious family, only to realize the village has been trying to map itself onto him.
5. The Twin in the Wall
After her twin sister’s death, a woman moves into their childhood home to settle the estate and starts hearing her sister’s voice through the walls, giving her small, helpful warnings, each one true. She isn’t sure whether she’s being protected or slowly replaced.
6. The Choir of St. Agnes
A restoration architect is hired to repair a fire-damaged church organ and finds that playing certain notes summons a choir no one else can hear, singing hymns older than the church itself, always one verse further along than they should be able to know.

Good observation! Honestly, a few reasons:
The AI model itself skews contemporary — the aesthetic defaults of current video AI (clean kitchens, white shirts, shallow focus, moody underlighting) are trained heavily on modern commercial and streaming content, so the visual language it produces naturally echoes directors who are prominent now.
The styles it can replicate are ones with lots of training data — Fincher, Villeneuve, Garland etc. have highly distinctive, widely discussed and documented visual signatures that are well represented online, which is exactly what AI models learn from.
Noir and classic cinema is harder to prompt — older directors like Kubrick, Cassavetes, Tarkovsky, Bergman, or Ophüls had styles rooted in film grain, anamorphic lenses, and practical lighting that AI video currently struggles to authentically reproduce. When you get B&W it tends to look like contemporary B&W (clean, digital) rather than genuine 1950s or 1960s celluloid.
I was also pattern-matching to what felt plausible — since this is AI-generated footage, it made sense to name directors whose work the model might plausibly have “absorbed.”
If you wanted to push toward older directors — say Kubrick’s symmetry, or Fellini’s chaos, or Bresson’s austerity — it would be interesting to see how hard you’d have to work against the model’s defaults to get there. Have you tried prompting for specific older styles?
Interesting comparison’s – some are a bit wide of the mark in terms of accurately connecting them with a director, but mostly genre remains accurate. In terms of the references, it’s interesting that (in particular the BW films) Hitchcock, Carol Reed, even David Lynch for the more surreal ones.
I don’t know yet what this has told me. Mainly that the models being used for image generation are probably/possibly skewing towards newer, more prevalent styles and media. This may mean that the influence of individuals, or of older media may not be acknowledged, and the canon of influence may not be seen or mapped. In comparison to older versions of appropriation, where the work is ripped and kind of acknowledged. Does this mean it’s not being critical, influenced by something generated obfuscates the lineage and critical position of a movement?
Discussed this with friends, we spoke about knowing the provenance of a film. It turned to epistological arguaments – what’s the difference between machine knowing and individuals knowing.

Bodies in digital transition presentation notes 
INTRO 


Introduction to who I am, practice-based PhD, Arts and Computational Technology,  Goldsmiths 


V Short introduction to my practice, focusing on personal practice: a magpie-ish relationship with style, often moving between registers e.g. performance work with Irini which copied copy-pasta, video work focused on the gothic and medicine, folk tales and 


Interest in authorship, collective authorship:  


In-grid works with collective authorship, and uses a lot of collective writing practices 


Working under pseudonym (G George) 


Interested in that as 1. a freeing practice 2. a communal practice 3. how borrowing visual and textual signifiers can shortcut to understanding 


Introduce basis of PhD: how authorship can be conceptualised when working with techniques including appropriation and pastiche, and how working with AI-generated content complicates these issues further. 


THE MEAT 


Propose reading this condition through the gothic: a genre historically preoccupied with unstable authorship, from Walpole’s fraudulent framing of The Castle of Otranto as a found manuscript onward, and with architectures of hidden, unindexed space, doubles, dopplegangers and secret histories. (see also the Woman in White, The King in Yellow, Frankenstein, Dr Jekyll & Mr Hyde etc) 


Short overview of why I’m interested in the gothic and how it is defined:  


Cross disciplinary: Film, literature, fashion, music 


Slippery in definition, and difficult to apply to visual arts 


Horror community and fan culture, space for the queer uncanny 


The economics of horror 


Specific gothic tropes of generational secrets, misauthored/misinterpreted text, obsession, recurrance (history repeating itself), doubles and dopplegangers 


Artifice and theatricality, deliberate gaslighting/misleading of the protagonist 


Can these tropes be pivoted to describe something happening in generative system assisted works? 


Linking to genAI and authorship  


Style and trope surfacing in GenAI output with no traceable citation or intent behind them 


Not framed as theft or loss, framed as strange, genuinely uncanny: a return without a returning subject 


Appropriation/pastiche/détournement are knowing practices with articulated relations to source; fan cultures copy communally and citationally; GenAI’s recurrence has neither of these features. It’s a different kind of copying, and does that have its own potentials?  


Rather than treating this only as a loss of authorial control, I want to ask what it opens up. Can this ownerless recurrence be redirected into appropriation in its fullest sense, as deliberate remix or détournement? Can GenAI become a tool for productive misreading rather than passive extraction? 


In a system which is obscured from us – a castle of locked doors and empty crypts – can we make something in the gaps? 


This difference in practice and potential practice is the interesting object, not a verdict or a moral position. 


CONCLUSION 


Finish in a space of uncertainty: is this something to mourn, exploit, ignore, notice? 


Can this be directed like detournment or does this import too much intentionality on an opaque process  


Open questions:  


Where’s the line between an artist’s generative process (however loosely I control it) and something closer to appropriation, when I can’t see inside the model? 


Does calling this “gothic” romanticise infrastructure that is extractive? 


Can a practice of détournement exist without a stable object being détourned? 


What would it even mean for a generative system to cite?

PhD/ReadingNotes/Notes----A-SemanticSynt.content:
aside Maybe I need to do more reading around semiotics?


                  
                   Altman-SemanticSyntacticApproachFilm-1984, p.image 3
                  
                


Now, one of the most striking aspects of Saussure’s theory of language is his emphasis on the inability of any single individual to effect change within that language. The fixity of the linguistic community this serves as justification for Saussure’s fundamentally synchronic approach to language.



Synchronic The similarity of observations within the same time frame. Concerned with something, especially a language, as it exists at one point in time. It is not about the similarity of things observed, but the observations.


                  
                   Altman-SemanticSyntacticApproachFilm-1984, p.image 4
                  
                


Unwilling to compromise their sytems by the historical notion of linguistic community, these theoreticians instead substituted the generic contextfor the linguistic community, as if the weight of numerous “similar” texts were sufficient to locate the meaning of a text independently of a specific audience.



Genre as audience specific, relying on the linguistic community reaching similar conclusions from a text/work, but not  taking into account their context.


                  
                   Altman-SemanticSyntacticApproachFilm-1984, p.image 4
                  
                


Instead of reflecting openly on the way in which Hollywood uses its genres to short-circuit the normal interpretive process, structuralist critics plunged headlong into the trap, taking Hollywood’s ideological effect for a natural ahistorical cause





                  
                   Altman-SemanticSyntacticApproachFilm-1984, p.image 4
                  
                


as Platonic categories



Plato loved categories, I think this is referring to his theory of moral forms.


                  
                   Altman-SemanticSyntacticApproachFilm-1984, p.image 5
                  
                


. By choosing the films it would patronize, the audience revealed its preferences and its beliefs, thus inducing Hollywood studios to produce films reflecting its desires. Participation in the genre film experience thus reinforces spectator expectations and desire



Religion and ritual - ritual approach accounts for the intensity of identification with fil, genre audiences. The question he then poses is, are studios presenting what consumers want, or are they molding the consumer identity through producing it? Did girl power birth the Spice girls, or did the Spice girls create girl power?


                  
                   Altman-SemanticSyntacticApproachFilm-1984, p.image 5
                  
                


Whereas the ritual approach sees Hollywood as responding to societal pressure and thus expressing audience desires, the ideological approach claims that Hollywood takes advantage of spectator energy and psychic investment in order to lure the audience into Hollywood’s own positions.





                  
                   Altman-SemanticSyntacticApproachFilm-1984, p.image 9
                  
                


Or take the development of the sciencefiction film. At first defined only by a relatively stable science-fiction semantics, the genre first began borrowing the syntactic relationships previously established by the horror film, only to move in recent years increasingly toward the syntax of the western.



This text outlines an alternative organisation of genre which combines semantic and syntactic approaches to genre. He posits that by keeping these approaches in opposition, three problems are caused: 1. there are opposing inclusive and exclusive cannons, one with set of semantic strict rules for a genre (films that take place in the american west in this time period are westerns) and one more syntatic approach which picks examples and revolves around that exclusive cannon. Altman’s formulation of semantic/syntactic argues that favouring one sort of definition over other creates the problem as these approaches are in fact complementary.
The second contradiction, which is the semiotic approach’s failure to address the historical foundations of a genre. Altman proposes two ways for how a given genre emerges: “either a relatively stable set of semantic givens is developed through syntactic experimentation into a coherent and durable syntax, or an already existing syntax adopts a new set of semantic elements” (558). In this sense, instead of treating genres as Platonic categories, Altman considers them historically and accounts for the industry’s impact.
This is where the third, and final, contradiction Altman discusses comes into play: two strands of genre criticism, the ritual and the ideological approaches.
This blog helped me understand it: u.osu.edu/english6778autumn2020/2020/11/30/altmans-genre-theory/

Trippy and trip wired (spooky and unreal, dangerous and psychedelic)

aside There’s something about the refusal to perform gender through pronouns that is tickling another area of my brain but I’m not sure what I mean yet. I’m thinking of writers who identify as female for instance, but use initials to obscure gender, this is not always a refusal but potentially a entrenching of those norms? I used G George as a pseudonym to appear as more than one person, but also it was assumed I was a man, regardless that George as a surname doesn’t suggest a gender. That was partly conscious. Thus, the glitch creates a fissure within which new possibilities of being and becoming manifest. This failure to function within the confines of a society that fails us is a pointed and necessary refusal. Glitch feminism dissents, pushes back against capitalism.

Being indefinable, unclassifiable. I find this difficult, because I like topologies in the same way I like organising materials, and objects in containers. I know however there is a freedom in messiness. I just never know where I’ve put anything.

Research through design / prototyping — building successive artefacts where each prototype tests a proposition. Distinguish exploratory prototypes from ones designed to answer a specific question; examiners look for that.
Material thinking / thinking-through-making (Bolt, Carter) — the argument that handling the medium generates knowledge unavailable by other means. In digital work this means the specific affordances and resistances of your toolchain.
Autoethnography — first-person account situated in a cultural context. Useful, but needs a clear analytic frame or it reads as memoir.
Speculative and critical design / design fiction — artefacts as arguments about possible futures rather than solutions.
A/r/tography — artist/researcher/teacher identities held together; strongest if teaching is part of your practice.

Methods for gathering data around the work

Audience and participant studies — observation, think-aloud protocols, interaction logging, video analysis of engagement, exit interviews. Standard for interactive installation work, and the thing most often done too thinly.
Semi-structured interviews — with other practitioners, curators, technicians, participants.
Elicitation methods — showing participants the artefact, footage or their own interaction data to prompt reflection.
Case study — of other artists’ works, of your own project, or comparative.
Practitioner-expert critique / peer review sessions — documented crits treated as data rather than as informal feedback.
Exhibition as method — the show as a designed research event with defined conditions, not just dissemination.

Analytic methods

Thematic analysis and grounded theory coding — for interview and reflection data.
Interaction analysis of video and logs — micro-level examination of what people actually did.
Contextual review — the art-and-design equivalent of a literature review, covering works, exhibitions and artefacts alongside texts.
Practice mapping / visual methods — diagrams, matrices and taxonomies as analytic instruments, not illustrations. Gray & Malins is strong on this.
Media archaeology / software studies readings — analysing the technical substrate as culturally loaded.

Framing and documentation methods

Documentation as method (Mäkelä, Nimkulrat) — deciding what to capture, when and in what form, as a deliberate methodological choice. For time-based and software work this is load-bearing.
Triangulation across modes — Nelson’s point that practice, documentation and writing each evidence different things, and the claim rests on their convergence.
Portfolio or exposition structure — the Research Catalogue’s exposition format as a way of presenting multi-media evidence.

Identify Keywords: Break your topic into main concepts and list synonyms, alternative spellings, and acronyms for each.
Boolean Operators (AND, OR, NOT):

AND narrows results (e.g., diet AND obesity).
OR broadens results with synonyms (e.g., teenager OR adolescent).
NOT excludes irrelevant terms.


Phrase Searching (” ”): Use quotation marks to find exact phrases, such as "global warming" or "climate change".
Truncation/Wildcards (*, ?): Use a symbol (often *) to find word variations (e.g., educat* finds education, educate, educational). Use ? for single character variations (e.g., m?n for man or men).
Nesting (Parentheses): Group synonyms together with OR inside parentheses to combine them with other concepts (e.g., (cancer OR tumor) AND therapy)

Intro: Lets learn some syntax!
This page is taken directly from Batool Desouky and George Simms’ Obsidian tutorial series github.com/sunSeekingGoth/MakeSenseWithObsidian

What is Markdown
It is a way to format your text while you are typing. It’s a more readable syntax-based code (technically a coding language) that is used within many websites (eg wikipedia) and web-building tool (eg Wordpress, pico).
Markdown is saved as .md files.
Because Obsidian is essentially a text editor, understanding Markdown syntax is the first step to getting comfortable. You can always come back to this section as a reference, so don’t feel like you have to remember everythingggg!
Official docs are HERE but we will run through the basics:

1 Headings
2 Styling
3 To Dos
4 Code!
5 Notes*Comments
6 There are many types of links 🔗
7 Embedding links
8 Tagging
 Properties
10 Why organise like this?



                  
                  Using this vault 
                  
                

We have set it up to try and make all syntax understandable and navigable. Usually Obsidian collapses syntax, but we have repeated things so you can see the markdown in code blocks and how they render next to each other.



1 Headings!
Oh Headings!!
And Headings!!!
That enable you to break up notes into sections and structure many levels of subheadings.
For organising
# ngs!
jam
small jam

2 Styling
BOLD
**BOLD**
Italics
*Italics*
Highlighted
==Highlighted==
Strikethrough
~~Strikethrough~~

3 To Dos

  something to do!

- [ ]
They help mark progress, and as we will see later can work in many adaptive ways.

4 Code!
Blocks 💻
pip install cute-things
using ``` either side of the text.
Inline
Inline-Code
Using one ` either side of the text.

5 Notes * Comments

[! ] This is a Callout, used to make stand out notes * comments
Use this to make comments * notes that you want to be noticeable.
You can also use all sorts of normal formatting in here like this.

> [! note] Make stand out notes \* comments 
> Use this to make comments \* notes that you want to be noticeable.
> You can also use all sorts of normal formatting in **here** ==like== ~~this~~.

6 There are many types of links 🔗
Links are a core part of Obsidian! And they are all pretty flexible and handy, creating a wide range of possibilities.

External
Web Links
[Web Links](help.obsidian.md/Linking+notes+and+files/Internal+links)
To enable you to link to external websites and resources.

Internal links
Simple (Wiki Link):
00_Intro
Structuring your Tasks (expand)
anythinghdskfhslkdhas
| pipe
syntax:
[[<FILE_NAME>]]
e.g.
[[00_Intro#knowledge-base--research-collection|short word]]
Use this to  link to files within your vault. when you start writing [[ you will be prompted to search existing files you can link to.

Links to non-existent notes
Obsidian can create new notes from links, so that you don’t have to interrupt your process to create a new note.
Like if you are mid thought, and remember that this text connects to something else you were reading the other day. You can put square brackets around that to create a place holder for a new note.
I want to work on somehitng later

[! note] the title of the linked note and what appears in the sentence are diferent
You can give a link another name using the | symbol
[[Related Concept | somethine else]]
This keeps your sentence cohesive as note titles don’t always make sense in-line


7 Embedding links
This enables you to link to images and other sorts of information within the docs! It also means that multiple notes can share and link to the same image, saving space and time. It also means that it is fairly limitless what you can do when it comes to embedding which makes it very transformable and adaptable.

Embed Local Image
Embed Local Image
Embed Online Image
Embed videos
Embedding Websites in notes
Shared pads?


Embed Local Image

![[<FILE_NAME>]]
e.g.
![[cool pup.png]]
This lets you embed an image form your vault. You can also drag files in!

Embed Online Image

![](<FILE_URL>)
e.g.
![](farm8.staticflickr.com/7007/6684384907_b093c428b4_z.jpg)
This lets you embed images from online. I would recommend using local though as it is more stable, and uses less energy.

Embed videos

<iframe title="Access Server, American Sign Language  with Optional Captions" width="560" height="315" src="tube.systerserver.net/videos/embed/5249d4a1-852e-4dfe-8b4c-42bb2eeb656c" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen="" sandbox="allow-same-origin allow-scripts allow-popups"></iframe>

Embedding Websites in notes

e.g.
<iframe src="help.obsidian.md/Editing+and+formatting/Basic+formatting+syntax#Bold%2C+italics%2C+highlights" style="width:100%; height:500px"></iframe>

Create a new pad and use the share menu to get the embed code like above.

8 Tagging
This is similar to social media tagging, they are used to make content searchable.
You simply use a # and word to create tags between documents. These can beinline or in page metadata (info about a note).

Subtags
Tag can be nested! Think of having broader topics containing more specific ones:
meeting
proposal andlog ,meeting etc.

9 Metadata / Properties
Similar to tags, metadata can store information about your notes, but it can also store information about the file itself.

Properties are always at the top of the page, so the example is in the CS-Annotations file. You can add them through the interface provided, or code them in like these examples:
---
<protperty_name>: <property_value>
---
e.g.
---
type: demo
---

[! Tip]
In read view you can’t see the properties, so this metadata is best used for information that you don’t want to appear in-line with your text.


Common metadata:

Date created (usually automated with Templates plugin)
Title (can be automated by pulling from note name)
Alias
Author
Citation


Metadata “types”
In comparison to tags, metadata can also store different kinds of data, like dates and boolean (true/false) data (e.g. if a file is being edited or not).



                  
                  Note
                  
                

These property types can also by manually coded in if you prefer but the menu can help!



10 Why organise like this?
Structuring your notes with metadata, links, headings and tags is what makes obsidian (and other knowledge bases with similar capacities) so useful, as they enable you to connect and thread your notes together in multiple ways!
Throughout the workshop we will also see how these threads will  enable us to bring together different ways of accessing your notes and research into new formations and interfaces that can help us understand it and connect it in different ways.
The main thing we will be trying to show is how to make these processes easy, sustainable and adaptable for you to fit around your practice and rhythms.

PhD/Writing/Literature-review-(20-30)/Li.content:
This research examines how fine artists use cinematic genre tropes and visual motifs in moving image work and photography, how authorship is conceptualised when working with techniques including appropriation and pastiche, and how working with AI-generated content complicates these issues further.
While the deliberate appropriation of existing images, styles, or motifs from other works and cultural sources is a well documented creative method, this approach appears to be an increasing aspect of works which use prompt based and generative ai systems as a tool. Rather than a deliberate critique or contextualisation of the original materials, AI image tools often recreate the visual style of individuals and movements, potentially without the intention, or the understanding of the artist making a new work.  In the context of a technologically engaged visual practice, I’m interested in how artists approach copying, pastiche, homage, remix, appropriation, ripping, quotation and recontextualisation, and where the differences between these practices lie.
The following is a preliminary outline of topics for a literature review. Some sections are less robust than others, and should be refined over time.
Appropriation, copying and complicating authorship
This section works to define what I mean by appropriation in this context, acknowledging that anxiety about the individual artist and machinic reproduction is not new, and grounding appropriation as a method.
If we compare the intentional process of appropriation as a method to the modelling of a style via a model, are the critical possibilities of appropriation as an artistic method still present if the culture being pastiched is not visible?

Appropriation as a way of understanding how ownership, authorship and value is constructed
Meme and remix as a way democratise culture
Recontextualisation (detournement) as a method to create new meaning

Gothic horror
I have chosen gothic horror as the genre as the primary genre for investigation. ‘Gothic’ as a set of conditions can be applied to music, fashion, literature, games, films and subculture, with can contain further subgenres depending on the area like cyber goth fashion, new and neo gothic art, gothic romance literature. Gothic horror in itself is amorphous and cycles into popular culture often (see 2026’s The Bride!, MĀRAMA, 2025’s Frankenstein, Dracula A loves tale, Sinners (southern gothic), 2024’s Nosferatu).
Introducing this genre as a focus relates to my practice and personal interested in looking at gothic/horror and genre fiction/ing, and its use as a precursor to science fiction, speculative fiction, and its use as reactive (potentially reactionary) media .
Here I hope to introduce the definitions of gothic horror historically, contemporarily, in cinema and in art, noting that these areas bleed into one another constantly.
What’s the difference between gothic horror and horror for goths?
